# Set SELinux to Permissive Mode

21. By default, SELinux will already be enabled and set to “**enforcing**” mode.

NOTE: For now, the system should operate in "permissive" mode. Permissive mode will post an alert when a process would have been denied, but will not actually deny anything. In a later unit, SELinux will be set back to "enforcing" mode.

22. Edit the SELinux config file. Type the command: `su -c 'vi /etc/selinux/config'` and press <enter>.

23. Password: ISS316Security

24. Press the " i " key to enter INSERT mode.

25. Change SELINUX setting SELINUX=enforcing to SELINUX= permissive .

```
# This file controls the state of SELinux on the system.
# SELINUX= can take one of these three values:
#       enforcing - SELinux security policy is enforced.
#       permissive - SELinux prints warnings instead of enforcing.
#       disabled - SELinux is fully disabled.
SELINUX=permissive #
# SELINUXTYPE= type of policy in use. Possible values are:
#       targeted - Only targeted network daemons are protected.
#       strict - Full SELinux protection.
SELINUXTYPE=targeted
.
```

![](img/73be0eef2ceb12f43f3eb92c420134f5_20_0.png)

26. Save the changes and exit the file. Hit the escape key to exit from insert mode, then hit the “shift” & “:” keys to enter command mode. At the colon prompt in command mode, type `wq` to exit and save changes.

27. Check SELinux configuration and current mode. Type the command: `sestatus` and press <enter>.

```
[student@TargetFedora01 ~]$ sestatus
SELinux status:    enabled
SELinuxfs mount:   /selinux
Current mode:      enforcing
Mode from config file: permissive
Policy version:    24
Policy from config file: targeted
```

![](img/73be0eef2ceb12f43f3eb92c420134f5_21_0.png)

28. The computer's current status is *enforcing*, but upon reboot, it will read from the configuration file and change over to *permissive* mode.

# Provide Limited Sudo Access as Alternative to Logging in as Root User

**Note:** Enable and use 'sudo' instead of logging as the root user as a best practice for system administration access. This task does just that. However, to gain an understanding how users and groups can be restricted using sudo, users with sudo permission will only be granted certain permissions. Permissions not explicitly given by sudo will require root's password.

34. Edit sudoers. Type the command: `su -c 'visudo'` and press <enter>.

```
## Networking
Cmd_Alias NETWORKING = /sbin/route, /sbin/ifconfig, /bin/ping, /sbin/dhclient, /usr/bin/net, /sbin/iptables, /usr/bin/rfcomm, /usr/bin/wvdial, /sbin/iwconfig, /sbin/mii-tool

## Installation and management of software
Cmd_Alias SOFTWARE = /bin/rpm, /usr/bin/up2date, /usr/bin/yum

## Services
Cmd_Alias SERVICES = /sbin/service, /sbin/chkconfig

## Updating the locate database
Cmd_Alias LOCATE = /usr/bin/updatedb

## Storage
Cmd_Alias STORAGE = /sbin/fdisk, /sbin/sfdisk, /sbin/parted, /sbin/partprobe, /bin/mount, /bin/umount

## Delegating permissions
Cmd_Alias DELEGATING = /usr/sbin/visudo, /bin/chown, /bin/chmod, /bin/chgrp

## Processes
Cmd_Alias PROCESSES = /bin/nice, /bin/kill, /usr/bin/kill, /usr/bin/killall

## Drivers
Cmd_Alias DRIVERS = /sbin/modprobe
```

![](img/73be0eef2ceb12f43f3eb92c420134f5_23_0.png)

# Set the Permissions of a File to be Immutable

39. Set immutable flag on file. Type the command: `su -c 'chattr +i /etc/services'` and press `<enter>`.
